canonicalPosts.caption:
Like many people, I’ve been trying to get my head around AI in procurement. A post by Asmaa Gad this week really helped. Her Agentic AI Platforms Map (65 platforms, 10 categories, 2026 edition) brilliantly illustrates how crowded this space has become.

Given the number of platforms and categories, I wanted to step back and understand what they actually do. The discussion that followed provided the answer. AI platforms can broadly be viewed as operating across three layers:
- Orchestration: automating end-to-end procurement workflows (e.g. major Source-to-Pay suites such as Coupa, SAP Ariba, GEP)
- Domain Intelligence: generating insight within specific areas—spend analytics (Sievo, Rosslyn), contract intelligence (Icertis, Ironclad), supplier risk (Resilinc, Prewave)
- Data Access: the foundational layer—connectivity, supplier data, and infrastructure that everything else depends on (Palantir, E2open, One Network)

It’s worth noting that the major S2P platforms are increasingly bundling spend analytics and risk monitoring into their core offerings. So are these truly three distinct categories, or three overlapping capabilities? Perhaps the more useful question isn’t “which platform category do I need?” but “which capability will deliver the greatest improvement in performance?” For most teams, it’s the intelligence layer. The workflows already exist—genuinely understanding what you’re spending, with whom, and at what risk is where AI could close the gap first.

“We want a new system… but can it still do what the old one did?”

20+ years and I still hear this in almost every project.

It starts full of ambition:
“We want something modern, streamlined, fully integrated”

Then about 10 minutes later:
“Can it create that report we print every Monday”
“Can we keep that workaround?”
“Can it look the same?”

At this point I’m usually thinking… so you want a new system, but as a tribute act to the old one. 🤔 

And to be fair, it’s understandable. It’s human.

People don’t ask for the old system because they loved it. They ask for it because they understood it.

That slightly awkward process
That Excel report nobody trusts but everyone uses
That workaround no one admits owning

…they’re familiar. And familiar wins, every time.

The reality is:
New system projects aren’t really about replacing software.
They’re about replacing habits.
And that’s the bit that’s hardest to price, plan, or document.

Because software is logical. People… less so.

My default response is to go back to what my kids taught me years ago - "Why?" once you ask it a few times you can normally spot the reasoning behind it. Then you can start to address it!

Curious how others handle this balance…

👉 How far do you go to keep things familiar versus actually moving forward?

Has anyone thought about how AI could make their home life easier?

I'm sure everyone is getting a little sick hearing about AI and how loads of people are going to lose their jobs, personally I prefer to see it as a way to make us all a bit more efficient and remove some of the drudgery from our jobs.

I thought i'd take that principle and apply it to home life. I reckon I spend about an hour a week (usually on a Sunday morning) doing 2 things:

📌 Putting together a meal plan for the week that caters for everyone in the family, the days where we've got less time to cook, the days where one or many of us are out. People not liking certain meals etc 

📌 Building a shopping list from all of those recipes and working out what I need to get in the weekly shop.

So when incapacitated last week I spent a couple of hours in an evening having a play with Microsoft Copilot to see if I could save myself some time.

This is only a simple prototype but already looking useful.

I've got a spreadsheet saved in OneDrive (I could point it at favourite recipe websites if I wanted) which i'm starting to populate with all of the recipes we use. There are a series of columns with key information. I might expand this a bit for example "Types of Meal" - Hearty, Light, Summer etc. I could maybe even get it to check the weather and suggest BBQ if weather and time permits 🤔

I've given it a series of instructions to mix up the protein and carbs during the week, to only have so many "Bad" meals (I might change this to a points system and set a maximum number of points per week). It pays attention to who is in/out on any given night and might suggest meals that one particular person isn't fond of if they're not around. I can say that i've got some ingredient that I particularly want to use up and it will add in recipes including that.

It then produces a meal list which I can tweak as I wish. Once the meal list is finalised I can then prompt it to groups all of the ingredients together and gives me a summarised shopping list. I've not yet got this pushing into a separate list as I like to check what I've got in fridge/cupboard/freezer etc first.

It's only in the early stages with a handful of recipes but as I build it up I reckon it's going to save me about 45 minutes a week and a lot of stress!!

Anyone else doing cool personal things with AI in their personal life?

Learning to pass an exam vs learning to do a job.

It's a real issue, for some reason when people set exams they often do it from a very literal "follow the rules" way and not from a practical real world experience approach.

There are certain exams that we take in our industry that show you know your way around Business Central. However, what they don't show is that you know how to deal with customers, question why people are trying to do something, and ensuring you can set the system up in an appropriate way.

I know someone studying for the MB-800 exam and thankfully they've picked up how badly worded the questions are and how they expect you to answer. They've also pointed out that it isn't how they would do it in the real world. That's a relief! The difference between text books (or Learn websites) and real world is huge. 

A couple of examples below:

In the first i'd always be questioning why they're trying to post to the blocked dimensions rather than just ploughing in and unblocking them. It might be legitimate but in my experience a lot of the time it's end user error.

In the second I honestly had never noticed that the page was called "Edit Dimension Set Entries" - you click the Dimensions action to get to it. And then the final point about "Implementing Codeunit 408" is bizarre, you don't implement it, it's standard functionality, it's just there and baked in to the system.

If you have to sit any of these Microsoft exams (or anyone elses) what are your biggest frustrations with them?

85% of leaders regretted a major decision last year.

I've coached 650+ CEOs.
Every one of them has been there.
And I have too, of course.

The decision that keeps you up at 2am.
The one you overthought until the window closed.
The one you rushed when you should have slowed down.

The gap between a good call and a costly one is preparation.

The best CEOs pick their decision tool before the pressure hits.

7 decision frameworks worth keeping close:

1/ The Eisenhower Matrix
→ Sort by urgency and importance
→ Do it, schedule it, delegate it, or delete it

2/ The OODA Loop
→ Observe, Orient, Decide, Act
→ Built for fighter pilots. Works for fast markets.

3/ One-Way vs. Two-Way Doors
→ Reversible? Move fast.
→ Irreversible? Slow down.

4/ The ICE Method
→ Score options by Impact, Confidence, and Ease
→ Pick the highest score. Stop debating.

5/ The SPADE Framework
→ One person decides. Everyone else is heard.
→ Kills the "who's actually in charge" problem.

6/ The Premortem
→ Assume the decision already failed
→ Work backward. Fix it before you commit.

7/ The 10/10/10 Rule
→ How will you feel in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years?
→ Strips the emotion out of the decision.

That last one is the one I lean on most.

10 minutes in, you're scared.
10 months later, you're glad you did it.
10 years later, you've made that call 20 times.

You're bulletproof.

What's your go-to framework for tough decisions?

Now that the World Cup is over, the heatwave has broken it feels like we're getting back to normal... or at least a different kind of chaos now the kids have broken up from school. 😄

Amongst all the distractions last week, I stumbled across a piece of functionality in Business Central that genuinely made my day.

One of the biggest benefits of a SaaS ERP system isn't just that it's hosted in the cloud and you don't need to worry about managing servers. It's that the product is constantly evolving, with Microsoft delivering new features and improvements every release.

A customer contacted me because they needed a user to access a very specific area of Business Central, but their current permissions didn't allow it.

Permission management has always been one of those areas where shortcuts can come back to bite you later. I've never been a fan of creating lots of bespoke permission sets. They can become difficult to maintain and often create problems down the line. At the same time, assigning a standard permission set isn't always ideal because it can grant far more permissions than the user actually needs.

The real challenge has often been working out which permission set gives access to a particular page or table without spending ages digging through documentation and settings.

That's where a feature introduced in the April release of Business Central comes in.

The Permissions Overview page allows you to enter a page or table and instantly see which permission sets provide access to it. Better still, you can immediately review everything else that permission set grants access to.
What used to be a frustrating and time-consuming task now takes a couple of minutes.

It's not the sort of feature that grabs the headlines, but these are often the improvements that make the biggest difference day to day. They help consultants, administrators and support teams make better decisions, avoid unnecessary customisation, and keep systems easier to manage in the long run.

Sometimes it's the little things that make you appreciate just how much Business Central continues to improve with every release.
Have you come across any hidden gems in recent Business Central updates?

"𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁 𝘂𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗱𝗮𝘆?"

It's a question I've been asked quite a few times by customers considering moving to Business Central SaaS.

The answer is update windows.

For our customers, we configure maintenance windows so Microsoft knows when updates can be applied with the least disruption to the business.

One of our customers was due to receive a production update last night. The update started as planned, but something interesting happened.

The monitoring systems determined that the update wasn't going to complete within the agreed update window. Rather than overrunning into business hours and causing potential disruption, Microsoft automatically stopped the update and rolled everything back.

This morning the system was fully available and the customer could carry on working as normal.

It's one of those behind-the-scenes features that most people never see, but it highlights the amount of engineering that goes into running a modern SaaS service.

When people think about Business Central SaaS, they often focus on new features, automatic upgrades and not having to manage servers.

For me, it's also about things like this. The safeguards that make sure updates happen at the right time, in the right way, and don't get in the way of the business.

Not the most glamorous feature, but definitely one of the most important. 👍

☑︎ Plans, builds and tests its own work.
☒ Twice the price of Opus for the same quality.

Use it for: long agentic builds you leave running. Anthropic says Fable on low effort often beats older models on Extra.

Every model except Haiku has an effort dial:
Low, Medium, High, Extra, Max. High is the default.

Here's where the bang for your buck actually is:

1. High is the sweet spot. Anthropic calls it the best balance of quality and token efficiency.

2. Medium is the cost step-down. On Sonnet 5 it matches Sonnet 4.6 at high.

3. Low is for bulk, classification and quick lookups.

4. Extra is for long agentic runs over 30 minutes.

5. Max is the trap. Anthropic's own words: significant cost for relatively small quality gains.

Start with Opus 5 on High.

Move the dial before you move the model.

"Can it be as simple as our current system?"

I had this during a recent Business Central demo. The operations team could immediately see the benefits. Better visibility, more integrated processes and a platform that could support the company's growth plans.

The finance team were less convinced.

Their current system is easier.

And to be fair, they're right.

The challenge is that their current system is a finance system. It does finance really well, but it was never designed to manage the wider business processes that the company now needs.

As businesses grow, processes become more complex. More people. More transactions. More stock. More projects. More reporting. More integration.

There's a common misconception that a modern ERP should be able to handle all of that complexity whilst remaining as simple as an accounting package designed for a much narrower purpose.

Unfortunately, business processes don't become simpler as a company scales.

The real goal isn't to make complex processes look simple. It's to make them manageable, visible and controlled.

Sometimes the easiest system today becomes the biggest constraint tomorrow.

What's interesting, though, is that we're starting to see technology come full circle.

With Copilot, agents and AI becoming increasingly embedded within Business Central, we're getting closer to a world where the complexity remains in the system, but users don't necessarily have to deal with all of it directly.

Instead of learning every process, users can increasingly be guided through tasks, have routine activities automated, and let the system do more of the heavy lifting.

The business still gets the capability it needs to scale. The user gets a simpler experience.

Maybe the question won't be "Can it be as simple as our current system?"

Maybe it'll become "Can it be more powerful without feeling more complicated?"

And that's a much more interesting conversation.
